doc.title: Nick Brignola interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 28, 1997

title: Sitting in with Cal Tjader and Wes Montgomery on the West Coast
summary: On a family trip he sat in at the Black Hawk, was hired by Tjader, returned to live in San Francisco for six months, played with Wes Montgomery.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: I’m going to pause for a second — can we open the windows? I think we should it’s pretty hot in here.
Let’s see. Cal Tjader. You moved out the west coast?

No I was visiting the west coast. My parents decided to take a cross country drive, and last minute I decided to go with them. And I had heard about this music called “west coast jazz” so I wanted to check that out. So we arrived in San Francisco, my aunt and uncle lived there and we were staying with them, and I read about this place called the Black Hawk, which is where Brubeck got his start and Cal Tjader happened to be playing there. And I didn’t know who Cal Tjader was, but I went down there and took my horn. And it was a jam session on a Sunday as I remember it. And I walked in and walked right up to Cal and said, “I’d like to sit in.” He said, “Where you from?” and I told him. At the time he had Vince Guaraldi on piano, Al McKibbon on bass, Willie Bobo on regular drums, and Mongo Santamaria on conga drums.
And which horn did you have?

Baritone. So I sat in and I wound up, he hired me. There was a Cuban tenor player playing with him. And he was leaving to go back to New York. And Cal kind of all of a sudden liked the baritone sound, you know with the baritone and the vibes is a little bit different. So I played, oh I don’t know, I think I played five or six of those jam session things that they did. Because on the weekends he had his regular quintet and had their own thing without the saxophone player. But I got to play and all of a sudden people were coming around in San Francisco like the writers and the people from the San Francisco papers and all of a sudden I started to get like a little reputation but I came back to New York with my family, and then I said well I’m going to move out here. So the following year I did move out there, and I stayed about six months, and I worked. That’s when I, you know that album “Cannonball at the Jazz Workshop?” I was there. We used to play the Workshop. And I first got to play with Wes Montgomery. Because there was another group out there called The Master Sounds. Buddy Montgomery, Monk’s brother, and Wes’ brother, and Monk Montgomery played bass. Anyway they had a group and they kept talking about their brother Wes Montgomery from home who played great guitar and he was coming out to visit them. And he did. He came out and they put him with an organ trio — it was an organ, drums and guitar. So I went in and I was in the men’s room and Wes Montgomery came in and I knew who he was, so I said to him, “I know your brothers and I just got through playing with them.” And he said, “Well get your horn and come on up.” So I wound up playing with Wes. And then about a year later he was big time in New York. He was recording and he was Wes Montgomery. But they were great times out there. But the problem was there wasn’t enough work and enough —
what’s the word — inspiration or creative juices were not happening for me out there. I had to come back to New York so I did.
